meta.title: Linus Torvalds uses AI to debug an Intel GPU driver bug
meta.author: Yogthos

comments.author: tomsmeding
comments.text:
The debugging using AI is great, as this sounds indeed like a horrible issue to debug and it's great that the fix exists now and is in the kernel.

However.


"and I let the AI write the commit message above." While this is a pretty well-written commit message, and so I guess I cannot fault Linus for the result here, it still sits uncomfortable with me.

The comments introduced in the commit do the classical LLM thing (recently discussed on this forum too!) where the comment describes the change from the previous state rather than the why of the current state. Now, I don't read kernel code daily so I don't know what the conventions are, but if it's anything like normal coding style, this is unhelpful. Furthermore, the unhelpfulness (and verbosity!) of the comment is one thing, but what I dislike most is that clearly Linus thought this was good enough! And it seems the commit is on master, so it's not a to-be-reviewed commit either.


"My kernel has LLM output in it" is a ship-has-sailed situation, but it seems my kernel now has slop in it, and slop from Linus' hand. That makes me unhappy.

comments.author: sunshowers
comments.text:
I have a hook which bans Claude from writing comments. I get two benefits from it: my coworkers are no longer subjected to Claude's verbal diarrhea, and it slows me down in a way that I've found helpful. I get to spend a lot of time in the code itself, which has been invaluable at catching bugs or suboptimal designs, both in what it generates as well as pre-existing ones. (A recent example was that the LLM's first cut used a second associated type in Rust when it should have actually forced the two associated types to go together via a trait. The second associated type provided a degree of freedom that should not have existed.)

For me a lot of engineering discipline with LLMs has been deliberately introducing roadblocks like this. It works well — I think the code I publish now, both the LLM-assisted and the hand-written gnarliest bits, is the most careful code I've ever written.

comments.author: rondahlgren
comments.text: I’ve been considered a similar thing. The comments are low in signal, high in noise. The code, on the other hand, does what it does. I find the comments are irrelevant and also mislead future agents. It’s an ironic twist on the “comment my code? My code is self documenting” trope of the 2000s.

comments.author: tomjakubowski
comments.text: Out of curiosity, does feedback from the hook seem to have any effect on stopping the model from burning tokens to produce the undesired prose comments in future work? It would seem more useful if it worked that way as opposed to working as a filter on the output.

comments.author: sunshowers
comments.text: It does, yeah, for the rest of the session. Usually the LLM will spit something overly verbose out, get chided by the hook, then write much shorter comments that conform to the hook. Though I don't think there's a huge marginal difference in the number of tokens.

comments.author: cesarandreu
comments.text: It's possible that Linus is still in the honeymoon phase with AI output. It really does feel quite magical, at least until you start noticing the same repeating patterns everywhere and it begins to feel gross.

comments.author: epidemian
comments.text:
I was thinking along those lines too. At first i didn't notice these things on LLM output. Now i'm way more vigilant of this "explain the history of how the next line got to be what it is, when its behavior is now the corrected and obvious thing and doesn't need an explanation" comments.

I have of course added system prompts, code style guides, and any nudges that seemed reasonable, to try to steer the LLMs into a saner direction. I think some of it has worked, as the bots sometimes mention writing comments following the project style, but these things are so stochastic that it's difficult to say anything with certainty.

It's pretty ironic that these AIs are so good at understanding ("understanding") code that is poorly documented, convoluted, and sometimes even minified, but they still tend towards over-commenting the code they generate. Even if they'd have no trouble understanding said code without those comments.

comments.author: wink
comments.text:
Did we read the same thing?


I'd like to call it my tireless helper, but the AI several times
stated flat out that this was impossible and unsolvable and that we
should just write a report about it.
I suspect those things have been trained by people who may not be
quite as stubborn as I am.
But while the AI was ready to give up several times, it did keep
adding debug code and analyzing it faithfully when I pushed


Doesn't sound like honeymoon at all to me, more like "I know this tool should help, but it takes some work".

comments.author: st3fan
comments.text: It is a high quality patch written by a domain expert so why would you call it slop other than to be negative and provocative.

comments.author: cuu508
comments.text: The commit message is not high quality and is not written by a domain expert.

comments.author: bmo
comments.text:
The comment you're responding to literally described exactly what is slop about the commit.

You can read the comments in the commit and judge for yourself but this style of over explaining what changed in code comments (which should be for explaining the current state, not your diff) is very common for slop that I see at work that hasn't been reviewed by the author. No one is saying Linus isn't being careful here with the actual change, but I agree with the comment that he's probably in the "honeymoon phase" and is being less critical of slop comments left by the LLM.

comments.author: sloane
comments.text: i got the sense they were referring specifically to the bad comments as slop, possibly the commit message. although they compliment the commit message explicitly, so i assume they are focusing on the sloppy aspects of this fix, not calling the entire fix slop.

comments.author: marcecoll
comments.text: I recommend you give up on this, there is nothing to be gained at this point with one side talking to the other. Let's focus on the things that we share. I am tired of everything being called slop, every thread being derailed by this but they aren't going to change.

comments.author: MarkMLl
comments.text:
The point has been made elsewhere that a commit message should address the patch from the POV of the project ("/This/ eliminates /that/ problem so please accept it as a patch") while there should be adequate inline comments for full understanding of the technical details.

By that metric there is too much in the commit message which should be in inline comments.

I accept that in this case it isn't very likely that the Linux kernel will be booted off GitHub and its trail of commit messages lost, but Poettering might have other ideas...

comments.author: intelfx
comments.text:
accept that in this case it isn't very likely that the Linux kernel will be booted off GitHub and its trail of commit messages lost


Huh?

How would "booting a kernel off GitHub" lead to losing "its trail of commit messages"? Especially considering that GitHub never was and never will be the primary (or, simpler, the only) place where Linux kernel is hosted (not to mention all the individual developers, who each has a full copy of the Linux kernel git repository, too)?

GitHub merely mirrors the repository (among many other places); it could be booted off GitHub today and nobody will be impacted.
